---
title: "Companion curriculum"
subtitle: "The teaching modules of the course"
---

The course is built around one exercise, taught on several cases: you reproduce a recorded result, vary the analysis behind it, declare one analysis before you run it, and read your result against those of the class. A short session or a single day has room for that exercise and little else, so the skills around it are taught in these eighteen modules, which run from a first line of R to a reanalysis that you can archive and version. Each module stands on its own, so you can take the one you need and leave the rest.

The modules share the cases between them. Each method is taught on the case that carries it best: the experiment of the housing-audit case for proportions, binary outcomes and conditioning on a consequence of the treatment, the survey respondents of the immigration-and-trust case for attitude scales, their reliability and survey weights in a regression on respondents, the cohabiting unions of the cohabitation case for censoring, the life table and discrete-time models of two competing ways out of a union, and the country-year panel of the EU-frames case for survey measurement, weights, panel models and a multiverse of hundreds of specifications. Where a module uses more than one case, it says at the top which sections work on which.

Nothing here is required for a one-day track or a short session, which run in full without any module and with no account to create. Each track points at some modules as optional preparation, at others as the slower companion of a task, and at the rest as reading for afterwards; the [last table](#sec-tracks) sets out which tracks use which modules. The longer tracks of the EU-frames case, over three days, a semester or self-study, are built out of the modules, and so is the semester track that takes the four cases in turn.

## Three strands {#sec-strands}

The eighteen modules group into three strands: the computational tools with which an analysis is written, the data management and sharing that let it be built and let others find it and run it again, and the statistical methods with which the cases are analysed. The strands are only a way of reading the curriculum, and you can read across them in whatever order suits you.

## Strand I – Computational tools {#sec-tools}

Three modules on the machinery of an analysis: the language in which it is written, the environment in which it is written, and the document format that holds the code and the prose about it in one file. The R module assumes no programming at all, and its first thirteen sections run their code on the housing-audit data, so that every result on the page can be compared with your own. The IDE module sets Positron, the default IDE of the course, beside RStudio and VS Code. The Quarto module displays its examples without running them, because it is about documents that you render on your own machine.

| Module | Level | What it covers | Cases |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Getting started with R](intro-r.qmd) | Foundation | What R and an IDE are; the console, the script and the report; objects, vectors and data frames, and why the mean of a 0/1 column is a share; installing and loading packages; reading data and looking at them; the pipe and the datawizard verbs; a share and a difference in shares; a first table, and a first figure with tinyplot and with ggplot2; a first call to `try_spec()`. Then, for a second reading: other file formats and fetching data from an archive; the three dialects of R; the grammar of graphics in depth; reading a specification curve; naming the estimand with easystats. | Housing audit (sections 1–13), EU frames (sections 14–18) |
| [Positron, RStudio and VS Code](ide.qmd) | Foundation | What an IDE does and what the course needs from one; Positron pane by pane, from the console and the Variables pane to the Data Explorer, Quarto, the Command Palette and Posit Assistant; RStudio and VS Code in brief, with what changes when you move between the three; six steps through a workspace that use every pane that the exercise needs. | Any; the steps use the housing-audit workspace, with the EU-frames variant beside them |
| [Quarto and reproducible documents](quarto.qmd) | Foundation | What a `.qmd` file holds and what rendering does to it; the header of the exercise report; the chunk options that the report uses, from `include` and `eval` to `error`; inline code; captions and cross-references; citations drawn from a `.bib` file; projects, folder settings and the freeze cache; publishing a finished document. | Any; the examples come from the housing-audit workspace and this site |

## Strand II – Data management and sharing {#sec-sharing}

Where data come from, how a downloaded survey file becomes the file on which a model is fitted, where finished work is deposited, how all of it is licensed, and how a piece of work is versioned and shared. The data of the housing-audit case are in the public domain and ship with the workspace; the panel of the EU-frames case was built from licensed Eurobarometer microdata and open World Bank indicators. In the course you complete the preregistration block of your report in Task 5, and the decks introduce archiving and version control, but there is no hands-on git work. These four modules take each of those topics further, and they are the ones to read once you have a question of your own to find data for, a survey file of your own to wrangle, or a report of your own to archive.

| Module | Level | What it covers | Cases |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Social science data sources](data-sources.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | The three routes by which data reach a researcher; a map of the survey programmes, archives and catalogues, household panels, official and administrative statistics, international indicators and political datasets, with the access rule for each; the sources of the EU-frames case step by step, with the GESIS download walked through screen by screen; citing data. | EU frames |
| [Building the analysis file](data-management.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | The two workspace scripts that turn your own sixteen GESIS downloads into the respondent file and then into the panel: checking files against the versions that the course used, harmonising the respondent characteristics, the three scoring rules, averaging into country-years with and without survey weights, and reproducing the committed panel to machine precision. | EU frames |
| [Reproducibility repositories](repositories.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | What a repository has to do; the generalist repositories compared; code forges and why a release needs a DOI; the package of the housing-audit study on the Harvard Dataverse and how a record keeps its versions; the SCORE dossiers of the housing-audit and EU-frames cases on the OSF, with forks and archives; the OSF after 2026; registrations and the preregistration templates behind the block of Task 5; an exercise in finding the record; a route for depositing a reanalysis of your own. | Housing audit, EU frames |
| [Git and GitHub for reproducible research](git-github.qmd) | Advanced | Version control from first principles; git on your own machine; GitHub, remotes, forks, templates and pull requests; what belongs in a repository and what never does, with a public-domain file and licensed survey microdata as the two examples; putting your own reanalysis under version control, one decision per commit. | Housing audit, with the licensed files of the EU-frames case |

## Strand III – Statistical methods {#sec-methods}

Eleven modules on the statistical side of the cases, roughly in the order of the ladder of difficulty: the design of an experiment and the models for a yes-or-no outcome; the causal graph that decides what to compare or hold constant; the survey items, weights and missing answers behind a scale; the event-history models of the cohabitation case; the panel models of the EU-frames case and its claim at the level of respondents; simulation as a check of a method; and the multiverse that every class builds. Each computes its numbers from the files of the course when the page is built, so a module can be read as a worked analysis as well as an explanation. The participant reading of the EU-frames case, [reading a specification curve](../cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd), belongs with this strand without being a module of its own.

| Module | Level | What it covers | Cases |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Audit experiments](experiments.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | Audit and correspondence studies of discrimination; what random assignment buys, with a check of balance; names as treatments; why a comparison among replies needs care, with a bound on how far a change in who replied could go; randomisation inference; power, and why significant estimates from small studies tend to be too large; the ethics of deceiving the people whom an audit studies. | Housing audit |
| [Binary outcomes](binary-outcomes.qmd) | Foundation to intermediate | A 0/1 outcome and its share; the difference in proportions and its standard error; the linear probability model with HC2 standard errors; logistic regression; odds ratios against percentage points and average marginal effects; why a covariate changes an odds ratio even in an experiment; then a survey item in clustered data: logit and probit side by side, errors clustered by country-year, the national unemployment rate between and within countries, an interaction, and a random intercept. | Housing audit (sections 1–7), EU frames (section 8) |
| [Causal graphs & adjustment sets](dags.qmd) | Intermediate | What a causal graph commits you to; confounders, mediators and colliders; why comparing greetings among replies conditions on a consequence of the name; the graph of the housing-audit case and what counting every delivered email changes; graphs written as `dagify()` formulas; a collider in a regression; the EU-frames graph, whose adjustment set is what two-way fixed effects absorb, and what fixed effects cannot fix; what no statistic computed from the data can settle; your own graph. | Housing audit (sections 1–6), EU frames (section 7) |
| [The items behind the scales](measurement.qmd) | Intermediate | The instrument behind every outcome of the EU-frames menu: how the four framing scales and the two composites are built from thirteen items; how often each item is named and how the items hang together; exploratory and confirmatory factor structures; what a two-item scale can and cannot support. Then the scales of the immigration-and-trust case: the three items of concern about immigration and their index; Cronbach's alpha of each scale, and why a single item weakens the coefficient; the two rules for unanswered items; the three trust items, why the paper keeps them apart, and what the choice among them, or their mean, does on the curve. | EU frames (sections 1–9), immigration and trust (section 10) |
| [Weights](weighting.qmd) | Intermediate | Survey weights inside a country-year cell, precision weights across cells and population weights across countries; why only the third changes the estimand; the reproduced coefficient under every combination of the weighting choices. Then the design, post-stratification and population weights of the European Social Survey in a regression on respondents: what each makes the estimate describe, the coefficient as an average of one slope per country, and why three of the five uses of the weights stay on the curve of the immigration-and-trust case. | EU frames, immigration and trust (last section) |
| [Missing answers](missingness.qmd) | Intermediate | What a respondent who mentions no frame at all does to a share built from mentions; the rules that the menu offers and what each assumes; multiple imputation with mice and Amelia, pooled by Rubin's rules, against the fiat rules; a sensitivity band. | EU frames |
| [Event-history analysis](event-history.qmd) | Intermediate | Time to an event and censoring, and why the share married by the interview mixes the event with the time that each union was observed; the life table, the hazard, and marriage and separation as competing events; person-period data; the discrete-time logit and its baseline of time since the start; the complementary log-log model, the proportional hazards model for time measured in whole months; competing risks with a multinomial logit; period against cohort. | Cohabitation |
| [The statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd) | Foundation to advanced | Every model fitted on the panel, output by output: why the analysis sits at the country-year level; a first linear model; clustered standard errors and the CR2 correction for few clusters; the two fixed-effects designs; within and between, with random effects and the within–between model; person-level multilevel models; survey weights; Bayesian estimation; bounded outcomes; effect sizes on one scale. | EU frames |
| [The individual level](individual-level.qmd) | Advanced | The claim fitted where its author fitted it, on a simulated person-level dataset validated against the real respondents: individual circumstance against national context, what the levels of a multilevel model do to its degrees of freedom, and the second claim of the paper under three designs. | EU frames |
| [Simulation as a method](simulation.qmd) | Intermediate | Data with a known recipe: parameter recovery, composition against context, weights that matter, the degrees-of-freedom argument run live, a null multiverse, a lineup, and design precision by simulation. | EU frames |
| [The multiverse and its critics](multiverse.qmd) | Intermediate | Where multiverse analysis came from; the three purposes that a multiverse can serve; the debate of 2025–26 read against a small curve on which every specification agrees and a replication still failed; robustness against replicability; the multiverse in teaching; then the same debate on a curve of hundreds of specifications, with the estimator as a fork of estimands and the displays of heterogeneity and influence. | Housing audit (sections 1–8), EU frames (section 9) |

A short session and a one-day track have room for the exercise and a few slides of background, so they use the modules mainly for preparation and for afterwards. During the day itself, the one-day tracks of the housing-audit, immigration-and-trust and cohabitation cases point at the causal-graphs module in Part 2 and at the multiverse and repositories modules in Part 4, and the day of the cohabitation case at the event-history module in Part 3 as well. The longer formats are built out of the modules: each three-day course, on [immigration and trust](../tracks/trust-three-days/index.qmd), [cohabitation](../tracks/cohabitation-three-days/index.qmd) or [EU frames](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/index.qmd), takes the modules that its case needs, and the [self-study track](../tracks/self-study/index.qmd) uses every module, each in the stages of the case that carries it.

## A first route through {#sec-route}

If you are new to all of this and want a route through, take the modules in this order, which is also roughly the order of what each one assumes. Sections that work on a case you are not studying can be skipped without losing the thread.

1. **Before the course: [Getting started with R](intro-r.qmd), sections 1 to 13, then [Positron, RStudio and VS Code](ide.qmd).** Arrive able to read a data frame, a pipe and a dplyr chain, and knowing where the console, the variables and the data viewer are in the IDE that you chose, so that the tasks are about the ideas rather than the syntax.
2. **Before or after the course: [Quarto and reproducible documents](quarto.qmd).** The report that you fill in is a Quarto document, and this module explains every option that it uses.
3. **Either side of the course: [Audit experiments](experiments.qmd), then [Binary outcomes](binary-outcomes.qmd).** The design that makes a comparison of randomised groups an estimate of an effect, and the models for a yes-or-no outcome.
4. **Either side of the course: [Causal graphs & adjustment sets](dags.qmd).** The graph of Task 2 at a slower pace, in an experiment and in a panel.
5. **For the immigration-and-trust case: [The items behind the scales](measurement.qmd#sec-trust), section 10, [Weights](weighting.qmd#sec-trust), the section on the case, and sections 3 to 6 of [The statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd#sec-pooled).** An attitude scale and its reliability, the weights of a cross-national survey in a regression on respondents, and fixed effects, random intercepts and errors clustered by country, which that module teaches on the EU-frames panel.
6. **For the cohabitation case: [Event-history analysis](event-history.qmd).** Censoring, the life table, person-period data and the discrete-time models of two competing events. Read sections 1 and 2 before Task 3 of the case and the rest after it, because Task 3 asks you to find out for yourself something that section 3 mentions.
7. **For the EU-frames case: [Social science data sources](data-sources.qmd) and [Building the analysis file](data-management.qmd), then [The items behind the scales](measurement.qmd), [Weights](weighting.qmd), [Missing answers](missingness.qmd) and [The statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd).** Where the data come from, the decisions made at the boundary between respondents and cells, and the panel estimators output by output.
8. **After the course: [The multiverse and its critics](multiverse.qmd), and for the EU-frames case [The individual level](individual-level.qmd) and [Simulation as a method](simulation.qmd).** The ideas behind the curve that the class builds and the arguments against them, then the claim at the level of respondents and data with a known recipe.
9. **After the course: [Reproducibility repositories](repositories.qmd), then [Git and GitHub](git-github.qmd).** The public records of the cases read as models, and the two modules that turn a report of your own into something archived, versioned and shared.

Read as much or as little as suits you. On a short session or a one-day track the course stands on its own, and the curriculum is there for when you want more, while on the longer tracks the modules make up most of the course. The [self-study track](../tracks/self-study/index.qmd) follows roughly this route, one case at a time.
